body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Adoption of biosecurity practices on dairy farms: a systematic review of barriers and facilitators","authors":"Van Rensburg-Okoli T, Brannigan-Sato M, Holmqvist-Adeyemi R","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Farm Animal Health Management","doi":"10.5555/jfahm.2021.0310","providerType":"review","abstract":"We reviewed 41 studies of biosecurity practice on dairy farms in temperate countries. Fewer than half of farms reported isolating purchased cattle, and footbath use, visitor controls and vehicle hygiene varied widely. Barriers most often reported were cost, time, farm layout and a belief that disease comes from neighbours rather than purchases. Facilitators were advice tailored to the farm, a trusted veterinarian and visible disease events nearby. Only six studies evaluated an intervention to increase adoption, and most measured practices by farmer report rather than observation."},{"title":"Quarantine of purchased cattle on dairy farms: a cross-sectional survey of 312 herds","authors":"Kilbride-Achebe S, Moreno-Lindahl P","year":2019,"venue":"Dairy Herd Health Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 312 dairy herds in two regions about how purchased cattle were introduced. Thirty-four percent of herds that had bought cattle in the previous year kept them apart from the main herd for at least three weeks, and 12 percent tested them before mixing. Larger herds and herds with a written herd health plan quarantined more often. Farmers who did not quarantine most often cited lack of separate housing and labour at busy times. The survey relied on farmer report and had a response of 44 percent."},{"title":"Veterinary-facilitated biosecurity planning and adoption of measures on dairy farms: a cluster-randomised trial in 60 herds","authors":"O'Donovan-Mbeki C, Lundgren-Asante E, Tamura-Fitzgerald H","year":2022,"venue":"Preventive Veterinary Practice","doi":"10.5555/pvp.2022.0147","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Sixty dairy herds served by four practices were randomly allocated by practice to a facilitated biosecurity planning visit, in which the herd's own veterinarian agreed three farm-specific priorities with the farmer, or to usual advice. At 12 months, observed adoption rose by a mean of 2.1 of 12 measures in planning herds against 0.8 in usual-advice herds. The difference was largest for isolation of purchased cattle and visitor controls. Visits took a median of 2.5 hours including follow-up. Effects at 24 months were not measured."},{"title":"Why the advice stays on the shelf: interviews with dairy farmers about biosecurity","authors":"Rowntree-Oyelaran J, Castelli-Brandt A","year":2017,"venue":"Rural Veterinary Science","doi":"10.5555/rvs.2017.0065","providerType":"qualitative study","abstract":"We interviewed 28 dairy farmers about the biosecurity advice they had received. Most described advice as generic lists that did not fit their buildings or workload. Farmers trusted their own veterinarian more than leaflets or campaigns, but said advice was rarely followed up. Measures were adopted when they solved a problem the farmer had already seen, such as an outbreak on the farm or nearby. Several farmers said they would act on two or three priorities agreed for their farm but not on a list of fifteen."},{"title":"Measuring biosecurity on dairy farms: agreement between farmer-reported and observed practices","authors":"Haddad-Thorsen L, Mwangi-Beaumont K","year":2020,"venue":"Dairy Herd Health Reports","doi":"10.5555/dhhr.2020.0233","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On 85 dairy farms, a researcher observed 10 biosecurity practices during an unannounced visit after the farmer had completed a questionnaire about the same practices. Farmers reported isolating purchased cattle on 61 percent of farms, but isolation facilities in use were observed on 29 percent. Agreement was good for footbath presence but poor for footbath use and visitor controls. The authors recommend observed measures for evaluating biosecurity interventions and note that unannounced visits were acceptable to most farmers. Observation took about 40 minutes per farm, and two farmers declined the unannounced visit."}]}
